analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and lets uninsured people buy federal-employee health plans at full unsubsidized cost.
analysis.headline: The repeal-and-replace bill was referred to nine House committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and its companion reconciliation law, wiping out the insurance marketplaces, premium subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, protections for pre-existing conditions, and coverage requirements for insurers. In its place, the Office of Personnel Management would open federal-employee-style health plans to people not enrolled in Medicaid, Medicare, or employer coverage — but with no government contribution toward premiums, premiums varying by region, and a tax deduction for those who can afford to pay out of pocket.
analysis.who_benefits: Large employers would no longer face penalties for not covering workers, insurers would be freed from required benefits, pricing rules, and minimum medical-spending ratios, and higher-income households would gain a new deduction for premiums. A narrower group — uninsured people healthy or wealthy enough to pay full freight — could buy federal-employee-type plans.

how_it_helps.text: Any individual not enrolled in or eligible for Medicaid, Medicare, CHIP, or federal-employee coverage could buy a federal-employee-style health plan, giving some uninsured people a new option
Premiums paid for these plans would be deductible above the line for income tax purposes, reducing tax bills for people who buy the coverage
Repealing the health law would end employer-mandate penalties and the individual requirement to carry coverage

analysis.who_pays: Millions of people would lose marketplace subsidies and the Medicaid expansion, and people with pre-existing conditions would lose guaranteed-issue protections because the bill restores the law as it stood before 2010. The replacement plans carry no government contribution, so the people most likely to need them — sicker and lower-income households — would face full, regionally variable premiums in a risk pool kept separate from federal employees' pool.
analysis.who_pays_short: People losing ACA coverage and protections

drawbacks.text: The bill provides that no government contribution will be made for anyone enrolled, so the replacement plans would be paid entirely out of pocket, with no subsidies replacing the ones repealed

Repealing the ACA and the reconciliation act restores the law as it stood before 2010, ending the Medicaid expansion, premium tax credits, guaranteed issue, and required benefits such as the ban on lifetime caps
Rates and premiums may differ among geographic regions, so people in high-cost areas would pay more for identical coverage
Enrollees must be kept in a risk pool separate from federal employees, so sicker non-federal enrollees could not be buffered by the federal workforce's pool
The premium deduction is worth the most to higher-income households with larger tax liabilities, and does little for people who cannot afford premiums in the first place

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The new coverage option is real — federal-employee-style plans historically accept applicants regardless of health status, so some uninsured people could gain access. But the bill removes every funding stream the ACA provided to pay for coverage: no subsidies, no Medicaid expansion, no employer or individual requirements bringing healthy people into the pool. Most independent analysis of repeal-and-replace designs of this era found coverage losses concentrated among lower-income and sicker people, while the savings and deregulation flow to employers, insurers, and higher earners. The trade is heavily one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to nine House committees and three subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa introduced the bill on February 15, 2013; it was referred the same day to nine committees, with Energy and Commerce listed first

Over the following two months it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, the Health subcommittee again, the Indian and Alaska Native Affairs Subcommittee, and the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee
No committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever held, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still in committee

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The tens of millions of people whose coverage depends on the ACA — Medicaid expansion enrollees, people receiving premium subsidies, and people with pre-existing conditions — kept those protections, because the repeal never advanced. Employers, insurers, and higher earners gained nothing from the bill's death but lost nothing either, since the ACA remained in place.

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to nine committees

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to nine committees with jurisdiction split among them, leaving no single committee with clear ownership

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: First-listed committee of referral (with eight others)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the 113th Congress

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the single cosponsor were House Republicans; no Democrat joined, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: Repeal ends the individual and employer requirements that brought insurers millions of mandated customers, but also frees them from required benefits, medical loss ratio minimums, and pricing protections, so they could deny or surcharge people with pre-existing conditions again. The bill also lets OPM compel carriers to offer non-federal plans as a condition of their federal-employee contracts, a new obligation.
Repealing the ACA ends employer-mandate penalties and coverage reporting, saving large employers money. The cost falls on workers who would lose coverage or protections they had under the law.

The new above-the-line deduction for premiums is worth the most to households with high tax liabilities. It does not conflict directly with the public interest, but it is a tax benefit skewed toward those already able to pay premiums.

Repealing the reconciliation act would restore the Medicare Part D coverage gap that the law had been closing, ending manufacturers' discount obligations — a gain for drug makers — while reducing the number of insured customers from the Medicaid expansion. Seniors would pay more out of pocket.
